title: Real-Space Analysis of Two-Photon Polarization States in Type-II SPDC for High-Purity Polarization Entanglement
authors: Koji Taninaka, Takashi Kakue, Ken Morita
abstract: Spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) is one of the most widely used sources of polarization-entangled photon pairs, and understanding the generated biphoton state is essential for realizing high-brightness and high-purity entangled-photon sources. In particular, Type-II SPDC produces a biphoton wavefunction with a complex coupling between the spatial and polarization degrees of freedom owing to birefringence. In this study, we calculate the real-space distribution of the two-photon polarization state from the biphoton wavefunction of Type-II SPDC generated in a \b{eta}-barium borate (BBO) crystal. By identifying the spatial correlation direction between polarization and real-space coordinates, we designed aperture shapes that restrict the collection along this correlation direction. Through both numerical simulations and experiments, we demonstrate that such correlation-aligned apertures simultaneously achieve higher entanglement purity and improved photon collection efficiency. These results establish a practical design principle for optimizing aperture geometries based on the real-space biphoton wavefunction, providing a new approach to realizing high-purity and high-brightness SPDC entangled-photon sources.
summary: This paper investigates how the geometry of photon collection apertures affects the quality of polarization entanglement generated via Type-II SPDC. By analyzing the real-space biphoton wavefunction, the authors demonstrate that restricting collection along specific spatial directions maximizes entanglement purity while maintaining high photon flux. This establishes a practical method for designing superior entangled-photon sources.
main_problem: The study aims to optimize the collection geometry for Type-II SPDC sources to simultaneously achieve high polarization-entanglement purity and high photon-pair collection efficiency.
main_result: Designing apertures based on the real-space biphoton wavefunction, specifically by restricting collection along the direction of strong polarization-position correlation, improves the trade-off between entanglement purity and brightness.
method: The authors calculated the real-space two-photon wavefunction and analyzed its spatial dependence to guide the design of apertures, which were then tested through both numerical simulations and physical measurements.
model_or_system: The system is Type-II Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) using a BBO crystal, generating polarization-entangled photon pairs. The analysis relies on the complex coupling between spatial and polarization degrees of freedom due to birefringence.
key_observables: CHSH Bell parameter (S) for entanglement purity, coincidence count rate (Brightness), Amplitude Balance (C), and Relative Phase ($\phi$).
important_parameters: Aperture shapes (circular vs. slit/elliptical), and the spatial correlation direction derived from the biphoton wavefunction.
main_assumptions: The theoretical model assumes monochromatic pump, signal, and idler photons, which is noted as a potential source of discrepancy with the experimental results.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spatial dependence of entanglement diagnostics (C and $\phi$) and compare the Bell parameter (S) versus brightness for different aperture shapes (circular vs. slit), showing the slit's advantage.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical framework using the real-space wavefunction to analyzing the spatial dependence of entanglement diagnostics, culminating in experimental comparisons between different aperture geometries to validate the design principle.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, actionable design principle for optimizing quantum light sources by linking the fundamental quantum state structure (real-space wavefunction) directly to practical optical components (apertures).

Fig. 4. Experimental setup and aperture geometries used to investigate the effect of aperture geometry on polarization entanglement. (a) Experimental setup. Photon pairs generated by Type-II SPDC are transmitted through either a circular aperture (iris) or a slit aperture before being coupled into multimode fibers and detected by Si avalanche photodiodes. The Bell parameter is evaluated from coincidence counts between detectors A and B. A band-pass filter (BPF, 810 nm center wavelength, 10 nm bandwidth) is used to select photon pairs centered at 810 nm. (b) Circular iris and slit apertures used for the measurements.
